To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the Central Colorado trough is interpreted as a flexural foreland basin that was filled with Pennsylvanian and Permian sediments by syndepositionally thrust-related processes and (2) the Sangre de Christo Mountains are the result of post-Pennsylvanian– Permian deformation of the Central Colorado foreland basin.
Pennsylvanian to Lower Permian strata of Central Colorado trough record deformation and sedimentation of an asymmetric, thrust-bounded basin.

Pennsylvanian to Permian strata in the Central Colorado trough contain evidence for a thrust-related flexural basin that was asymmetric in cross section, and that the Sangre de Christo Mountains are the result of a complex history of deformation and basin evolution.
